fixes.explanation: Yes, that's it. The text says, “…the Spirit of God rushed upon him…” Saul has just come back from the field behind his oxen, and the news from Jabesh reaches him. Then the Spirit rushes upon him, and the text says he burned with great anger.
That's it, friend. The men of Jabesh say, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.” Nahash has laid siege to their town, and that's the offer they bring him.

Nobody offers to pack up and walk away. The men of Jabesh say, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.” The offer is a treaty and service. I'd have loved a simple ending too, but that's not what the text gives.
The text doesn't say they prayed here. What it says is that they all wept aloud. Prayer is a fair guess, but I'll only tell you what the verse gives.

Fear isn't what rushes upon Saul. The text says “…the Spirit of God rushed upon him…” This is Saul, Israel's new king, hearing the words from Jabesh. Something much bigger than a shiver comes over him.

The people were weeping, so sorrow is a natural guess. But the text tells us they wept, and it doesn't name a feeling for them. For Saul it says “…he burned with great anger.” That's a different reaction from the people around him.
Shame doesn't show up in this verse. The text says that when the Spirit of God rushed upon him, “…he burned with great anger.” BURNED, friend. That's not a word for a man staring at his shoes.

Yes, and the words are strong. Saul sends them out saying, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” Samuel is Israel's prophet (1 Samuel 3:20), and Saul puts his name right next to his own. Pieces of oxen are hard to ignore, friend.
That's the promise. The messengers carry it home: “Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.” That's a short wait. And when the messengers relay it, the men of Jabesh rejoice.

Seven days was what the elders asked Nahash for, back at the start. The promise sent home is different: “Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.” That promise names tomorrow, not seven days.
No moon shows up in this promise. The words are, “Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.” The sun is running this clock, friend, so the new moon can stay home.

That line would've been dramatic, but they don't say it to Nahash. Their words are, “Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you.” All he gets from them is tomorrow and coming out.

Yes, and they say it outright: “Bring those men here so we can kill them!” The people have just asked, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us?” and the men they mean are the ones who said it. That's a heavy thing to say, and Saul answers it next.

Right, he does not. Saul orders, “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” The people ask for one thing and Saul orders another. It's a heavy moment, and Saul's answer points to the LORD.
Samuel, Israel's prophet (1 Samuel 3:20), is part of this story, but Saul doesn't name him here. He says, “…for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” The salvation is credited to the LORD.

Yes, Gilgal. Samuel says, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” Samuel is Israel's prophet (1 Samuel 3:20), and he's the one leading the way. The people follow him there in verse 15.
Mizpah is a fair guess, but it's not the place Samuel names. He says, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” Gilgal is where he points them, so pack for Gilgal, friend.
Bethel never comes up in this passage. Samuel tells the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” Gilgal is the only travel plan on the table, so Bethel doesn't make the trip.

That's the word. The text says that after the peace offerings before the LORD, “…Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.” It's a big celebration after everything in this passage. Rejoicing greatly is exactly how it ends.

Mourning isn't how this passage ends. At Gilgal, they confirm Saul as king and offer peace offerings before the LORD. Then “…Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.” The text closes with rejoicing, not mourning.

Worry isn't what the text reports at Gilgal. The people confirm Saul as king in the presence of the LORD and offer peace offerings. Then “…Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.” The verse closes on rejoicing.
